Oil & gas · Uganda

Pipeline right-of-way and safety-zone mapping in Uganda

Uganda’s pipelines are entering decades of operation. PAU’s Midstream Regulations 2016 require written consent for any activity next to a pipeline, set precautions for work within 30 m of the right of way, let machines dig within 6 m of the pipe only under the licensee’s supervision, and oblige the licensee to survey its routes every six months. We give your integrity and land teams a dated, human-checked inventory of what lies in each band, and of what changed since the last survey.

Send your route for a proposal See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Between construction and decades of operation

Uganda’s first crude export pipeline and its oilfield feeder lines are moving from construction to operation, and a refined-products pipeline to the Kampala area is planned. Each is a right of way that has to stay clear for as long as the line runs.

“The right of way has been reinstated. Now it is being farmed and built on.”

Reinstated ground looks like any other field. New structures, gardens and fences appear on and beside it, and each is easier to deal with while it is new.

“Someone has been digging near the line.”

Ground disturbance next to a buried pipe is a safety risk before it is anything else. Fresh digging, spoil, trenches and new tracks show at the surface, and we flag them between surveys.

“The six-monthly route survey is due.”

The licensee owes PAU a route survey every six months. A dated register of what changed since the last one tells the survey team where to go first.

“Our lenders want evidence of what changed.”

Lenders and their environmental and social consultants need to know what has changed along the corridor between site visits. Dated, reviewed change maps give them the same record your land team uses.

What lies in the corridor matters twice: as a safety risk to the people living and working beside the pipe, and as a future compensation cost if structures must move. A dated record serves both.

Who this is for

  • Pipeline integrity and right-of-way teams
  • Land acquisition and resettlement teams
  • Environmental and social (E&S) teams
  • Lenders’ E&S consultants and monitors
  • EPC contractors and their land teams
  • GIS and asset-records teams

The bands in Ugandan law

What the Midstream Act and the 2016 Regulations draw around a pipeline

A summary of the public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

Rule What it says Instrument
Activity next to a pipeline “A person shall not undertake any activity in an area adjacent to a pipeline system without the written consent of the Authority, in consultation with the licensee.” The Regulations do not define the adjacent area Petroleum (RCTMS) Regulations 2016, S.I. 36 of 2016, reg 68
6 m, where there is no pipeline right of way No ground disturbance by anyone other than the licensee “within six metres from the pipeline system where there is no pipeline right of way”, without PAU approval. Ground disturbance includes excavating, digging, trenching, ploughing, drilling, tunnelling, backfilling, blasting, topsoil stripping, levelling, quarrying, clearing and grading Regs 91 and 2
30 m from the right of way Precautions to find out whether a pipeline exists before “any work … within thirty meters from the pipeline right of way”; 10 days’ written notice to the licensee and PAU before ground disturbance in the controlled area; locating and marking within 14 days; PAU’s response within 21 days; temporary fencing Regs 92 to 94
6 m from the pipe The pipe is located by hand before mechanical excavation within 6 m; after that, machines work within 6 m only “under the direct supervision of a competent person employed by the licensee” Reg 97
Crossings No vehicle or equipment crosses a pipeline except on the travelled part of a public road, without PAU approval Reg 98
Route surveys The licensee informs owners, occupiers and communities of the pipeline, with PAU’s approval, and “shall, survey the pipeline routes every six months” and report to PAU Reg 87(2), (7) and (8)
Safety zones A safety zone around every midstream facility, its extent set by PAU, in which “unauthorised vessels, vehicles, crafts, fishing gear or other objects shall not be present” Midstream Act 2013 (Act 4 of 2013), s.67
Upstream installations The same safety-zone scheme for upstream facilities EDP Act 2013, s.144

The six-metre rule in regulation 91 applies only “where there is no pipeline right of way”; near any pipeline, regulation 97 lets machines dig within 6 m only under the licensee’s supervision. We report each band separately, so your team can apply the rule that fits each stretch.

We report structures within 6 m of the pipe, inside the right of way and within 30 m of its edge by default, measured from the centreline and the right-of-way polygon you send. PAU approves a surveyed route within 30 days (reg 60); send us the approved route and we measure from it.

  • The Petroleum (Refining, Conversion, Transmission and Midstream Storage) Act, 2013 Act 4 of 2013 (Cap. 162) · 2013Safety zones around midstream facilities, their extent set by the Petroleum Authority of Uganda (s.67).
  • The Petroleum (Refining, Conversion, Transmission and Midstream Storage) Regulations, 2016 S.I. No. 36 of 2016, S.I. Supplement No. 14 to Uganda Gazette No. 39 · 2 June 2016Activity adjacent to a pipeline system (reg 68), the six-monthly route survey (reg 87), ground disturbance within 6 m where there is no pipeline right of way (reg 91), work within 30 m of the right of way (regs 92–94), mechanical excavation within 6 m (reg 97), crossings (reg 98).
  • The Petroleum (Exploration, Development and Production) Act, 2013 Cap. 161 · 2013The same safety-zone scheme for upstream installations (s.144).

Operating lines

A baseline, then scheduled re-surveys that feed the route survey

We buffer the route in its UTM zone, list each structure the review confirms with its distance to the pipe, its band and its chainage, and cut the route into 500 m stretches. Each stretch is rated for encroachment density: high where more than five structures stand inside the widest band, medium for one to five, low for none. It is a count that tells your right-of-way team where to go first, not a safety or integrity rating.

After the baseline, the route is re-surveyed on a schedule you agree with us. New and removed structures between dated surveys are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views, and your team receives a change notice after each survey. Fresh digging, spoil, trenches and new tracks near the line are flagged the same way, so the six-monthly route survey starts from a list of places that changed.

What you receive

  • A structure register: ID, distance to the pipe, band, chainage and coordinates
  • An encroachment-density rating for each 500 m stretch
  • New and removed structures between surveys, with before-and-after views
  • Fresh digging, spoil and new tracks near the line, flagged for checking
  • A change notice after each survey
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, Shapefile, GeoJSON and KMZ layers

New lines and sites

Route options, then a cut-off record

Before the route is fixed

For a new pipeline or a new facility, we count the structures along each candidate alignment or site, band by band, so the land and resettlement impact of each option can be weighed before the route goes to PAU for approval. See route and site selection.

At the cut-off date

Once the route is fixed, a register of the structures in the footprint on dated imagery supports the census, the valuation and the cut-off-date record under the Land Acquisition Act and the lender’s standards. See RAP cut-off-date baselines in Uganda.

After construction

Reinstatement, erosion and regrowth

Reinstatement and revegetation

How revegetation of the reinstated right of way, closed borrow pits and laydown areas is progressing, compared between dates.

Vegetation and land cover

Where vegetation has been cleared or has regrown on and beside the right of way, compared between dated surveys.

Slopes, drainage and erosion

Steep, erosion-prone and drainage-crossing stretches highlighted from elevation data, for your integrity team to prioritise, with drone elevation models for detail where flown.

Petroleum facilities

Well pads, processing sites, pump stations and terminals

Around a facility, the questions are what has appeared at the perimeter and inside the safety zone PAU has set, and what has changed since the last survey. We map new structures, cleared ground, new tracks and stockpiles in a ring around each site, compare them between dates and list them with their distance to the site boundary.

Your own plant, well pads and pump stations are never recorded as encroachment. The register shows third-party structures and land change around them, and your team decides what each one means.

Drone flights near facilities

Pump stations, processing facilities, well pads and storage sites fall under regulation 43 of the drone regulations, the operator’s own rules and CDF clearance. Satellite imagery covers them without a flight. See drone law in Uganda.

How it works

From your route file to a reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route, the right-of-way polygon if you have one, the districts the line crosses and what the record is for: the next route survey, a lender’s monitoring visit, a cut-off date or a new line. The bands, the imagery and the deliverables are agreed in a written proposal.

  2. Map from satellite

    Structures and ground disturbance are mapped along the whole route from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or imagery you already hold. Nobody travels to the line and no aircraft flies.

  3. Add detail where it helps

    Where a stretch needs more detail than satellite imagery shows, a drone survey is flown by a Ugandan operator under its own approvals, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result. Each feature is measured to the pipe and the right of way, placed in its band and dated, and the report and GIS layers go only to the contacts you name.

Who delivers petroleum work in Uganda

The petroleum national content regulations reserve land surveying, environment studies and impact assessments, and communications and IT services for Ugandan companies, registered entities and citizens, and suppliers to the crude export pipeline must generally be registered on PAU’s National Supplier Database. Where the rules reserve the work, it is delivered through a Ugandan partner or joint venture that meets them, or as a subcontractor to your appointed consultant or contractor, with our analysis, review and reporting unchanged.

Honest scope

What this is, and what it is not

What it supports

  • The licensee’s six-monthly route survey, with a list of what changed
  • Right-of-way management and community engagement, with dated facts
  • Lenders’ environmental and social monitoring between site visits
  • Cut-off-date and valuation records for new lines and sites

What it does not do

  • Detect leaks, taps, theft or the condition of the pipe
  • Replace in-line inspection, patrols or the licensee’s route survey
  • Decide whether an activity had PAU’s consent, or who is entitled to compensation
  • Serve as a cadastral survey: boundaries come from your registered surveyor
  • Map under cloud: optical imagery needs clear skies, so captures are planned for clearer spells

Onshore only: we map land along the corridor and around facilities, not open water.

Our work

What a register looks like

We have mapped structures along a high-pressure gas pipeline in Mozambique. This stretch of the sample was rated high: sixteen structures within 100 m of one 500 m stretch, each listed with its distance and band. A Ugandan register uses the same format, measured to the 6 m and 30 m bands or your own, and names the imagery used and its capture dates.

Frequently asked questions

Does your survey replace the six-monthly route survey the licensee owes PAU?

No. Regulation 87(7) puts the survey and the report to PAU on the licensee. A dated register of what changed along the route supports that survey and tells your teams where to walk first; it does not replace it, and it does not replace in-line inspection or patrols.

Which bands do you report along a Ugandan pipeline?

Whichever you set. The usual set follows the 2016 Midstream Regulations, within 6 m of the pipe and within 30 m of the right of way, plus the right of way itself, which you send as a polygon or as a width either side of the centreline. We add any width a lender, an ESIA or your company standard sets, up to six in one survey.

Can you tell us whether someone had PAU's consent for an activity?

No. Imagery shows that ground was dug, cleared or built on, and when; it cannot show a consent. Whether an activity next to the line was approved under regulation 68 or 91 is for your land team and PAU to establish.

Can you detect leaks, taps or oil theft?

No. Imagery cannot see a leak, a tap or the condition of a buried pipe. We flag what is visible at the surface, such as new structures, fresh digging, spoil, new tracks and cleared ground, for your teams to check.

Can drones fly along the pipeline?

Only with the approvals and security clearances each job requires. Every operation needs UCAA approval and Chief of Defence Forces clearance, and we read regulation 68 as needing PAU’s and the licensee’s consent for flights along a pipeline. Satellite mapping needs none of that.

Who sees the results?

Only the contacts you name. We never publish maps of your line or of the communities around it, and military and other sensitive sites are masked in every deliverable.

Send us your pipeline route

KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, and the right of way as a polygon if you have it. Tell us the districts the line crosses, the bands to report, the date the record must reflect and who receives the results, and we reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
